clue.text: Delivered book draft on time

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for book
a rough is a first draft
T stands for time, placed on the end

explanation.surface: A publisher's courier hands over a manuscript draft punctually.
explanation.definitionFit: Brought is the past tense of bring, a synonym of delivered when goods are carried to someone.

clue.text: Disney character: on reflection, hardly adult

parts.note: Bambi is the Disney fawn

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things back to front

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Musing that a Disney fawn is, when you think about it, scarcely grown up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on reflection' reads as 'thinking it over', but it turns the word on backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A bambino is an Italian word for a baby or young child, who is far from adult.

clue.text: Male-centred sporting policy associated with certain games

indicators.note: centred means placed in the middle of what follows
sporting suggests play and movement, so the letters are thrown about

parts.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A complaint that a sports policy favours men, linked to some competition.
explanation.definitionFit: Olympic is the adjective for the Olympic Games, so it means connected with those particular games.

clue.text: Haughty, awful pain, old Joanna

parts.note: grand can mean lofty or haughty in manner

indicators.note: something awful is in a terrible state, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Describing a stuck-up, unbearable woman named Joanna from the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joanna' looks like a person, but it is Cockney rhyming slang for piano; 'old' gives O to the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Joanna is Cockney rhyming slang for a piano, and a grand piano is the large concert kind.

clue.text: Thanks on capturing weirdly natural, scary creature

indicators.note: capturing means holding something within, so one part surrounds another

parts.note: ta is British informal for thanks

indicators.note: weirdly means in an odd, disordered way, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Gratitude for catching a strangely ordinary yet frightening beast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ta' is everyday British slang for thank you; 'natural' looks descriptive but is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarantula is a large hairy spider that many people find frightening.

clue.text: It could kill you to let go when on limb!

indicators.note: one thing set on another means the first piece is placed before the second in an across entry

parts.note: to fire is to let go, as with a gun or an employee
an arm is a limb

explanation.surface: A warning that letting go while dangling from a tree branch could prove fatal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Limb' suggests a branch you might fall from, but it is simply an arm.
explanation.definitionFit: A firearm is a gun, a weapon capable of killing, so the cryptic description fits.

clue.text: Member goes after sham, failed presidential candidate — no need to panic

indicators.note: going after something means coming later, so this piece is placed last

parts.note: false and sham both mean fake
Al Gore lost the 2000 US presidential election
an arm is a member, a limb

explanation.surface: A political report on a fake candidate who lost, with reassurance that all is calm.
explanation.walkthrough: AL is Al Gore, defeated in the US presidential race of 2000.
explanation.definitionFit: A false alarm is a warning that proves unfounded, so there was no need to panic.

clue.text: Artist's Sleep Activity/Mark Twain's Head

parts.note: REM, rapid eye movement, happens during dreaming sleep
a brand is a mark

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of Twain

explanation.surface: Reads like the slashed title of an artwork or exhibit, perhaps about Mark Twain's dreaming head.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals and slashes disguise the split: 'Mark' is not Twain's first name here but its own piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Rembrandt van Rijn was a Dutch Golden Age painter, one of the most famous artists.

clue.text: Ladies, say, in a rush, not in a friendly way

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: taken as written
to fly is to rush
the Ladies is an example of a loo, British for toilet

explanation.surface: Women hurrying past without a greeting, coolly unfriendly.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ladies is the British name for a women's public toilet, and loo is British slang for toilet; 'say' flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: Aloofly means in a distant, reserved manner, which is the opposite of friendly.

clue.text: Gold pieces first stuck on — how cute! — candelabrum

indicators.note: first sends the following word's equivalent to the front of the answer
stuck on means attached to the end, so this piece follows

parts.note: chess pieces are men
or is gold in heraldry
ah is the exclamation of fondness

explanation.surface: Admiring a candlestick with gold decorations glued on.
explanation.walkthrough: Or is the heraldic word for gold, and chess pieces are traditionally called men.
explanation.definitionFit: A menorah is the seven- or nine-branched Jewish candelabrum used in worship and at Hanukkah.

clue.text: A fashionable area might — just

parts.note: may and might both express possibility
fair and just are synonyms

explanation.surface: A tentative remark that some district could only barely count as stylish.
explanation.walkthrough: MAYFAIR is a wealthy, upmarket district of central London.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayfair is a famously chic, expensive London neighbourhood, an example of a fashionable area.

clue.text: Mock light with ring attached

parts.note: a lamp is a light
O is ring-shaped
something on is attached

explanation.surface: Describing an imitation light fitting that has a ring fixed to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mock' looks like an adjective, fake, but it is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To lampoon someone is to ridicule them through satire, which is to mock them.

clue.text: One's exercise with ball shows restraint

parts.note: one is I, so 'one is' becomes I'M
PE is physical education, school exercise
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Someone claims taking exercise with a ball demonstrates self-control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ball' suggests sport after 'exercise', but it is the dancing kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Impedance means hindrance or obstruction, so it is a kind of restraint on movement or current.

clue.text: Pass on after last of bone extracted from joint

indicators.note: something extracted is pulled out and removed from the rest

parts.note: a reefer is a cannabis joint

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter alone

parts.note: the final letter of bone

explanation.surface: A surgical or butchery picture: removing bone from a joint of meat before passing it along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' suggests meat or anatomy, but it is the smoked kind; take one E out of REEFER to leave REFER.
explanation.definitionFit: To refer a case or query is to pass it on to someone else to deal with.

clue.text: Rather large vehicle award

parts.note: OS is outsize, a clothing label for big sizes
a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: A prize consisting of a fairly big automobile.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oscar is the statuette awarded at the Academy Awards for film achievement.

clue.text: Study sound with eg mouth instrument

indicators.note: sound tells us to take the word as heard, not as written

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it at university
the mouth is an example of a body organ

explanation.surface: Advice to practise with a mouth-blown instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mouth instrument' suggests a harmonica, but 'eg mouth' is the organ piece; British students read a subject.
explanation.definitionFit: A reed organ, such as a harmonium, is a keyboard instrument sounded by vibrating reeds.

clue.text: People may wrongly believe this Burnham ground hosts Sunday cricket finals

indicators.note: something ground has been crushed and broken up, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: finals are the end letters of the preceding words

parts.note: the final letters of each word

explanation.surface: A rumour about a village cricket ground playing host to Sunday fixtures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like a cricket field after 'Burnham', but it is the past tense of grind.
explanation.definitionFit: An urban myth is a widely circulated but untrue story, something people wrongly believe.

clue.text: Above Uriah's deviance: not a way to conduct oneself

indicators.note: deviance is straying from the norm, so the letters wander from their order
not means leave out, here the single letter named

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, without the possessive

explanation.surface: A moral verdict that Uriah Heep's misconduct is beyond the pale.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove one A from the letters of ABOVE URIAH and rearrange. Uriah Heep is Dickens's oily hypocrite.
explanation.definitionFit: Behaviour is the manner in which a person acts, the way someone conducts themselves.

clue.text: English impertinence: every individual pinches Frenchman's bottom!

parts.note: sass is cheeky impertinence

indicators.note: to pinch something is to grip it, so one part holds another inside

parts.note: each means every individual one

indicators.note: the bottom of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the final letter of Frenchman

explanation.surface: An outraged complaint about cheeky behaviour where someone keeps pinching a Frenchman's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frenchman's bottom' is just its last letter. Sassenach is a Scots term for an English person.
explanation.definitionFit: Sassenach is a Scottish, often mildly derogatory, word for someone or something English.

clue.text: Second drink, Bordeaux?

parts.note: to sup is to drink
Bordeaux is an example of a port, the question mark flagging the example

explanation.surface: A diner asks for another glass of Bordeaux wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Bordeaux suggests claret, but it is the French port city; 'Second' is a verb, as in seconding a motion.
explanation.definitionFit: To second a proposal is to support it formally, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Austere box belt

parts.note: to spar is to box in practice
to tan someone's hide is to belt, or beat, them

explanation.surface: A plain, unadorned container and strap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'box' and 'belt' look like nouns but both are verbs of hitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Spartan means severely simple and frugal, after the disciplined ancient Spartans, hence austere.

clue.text: Sequence of Trump's initial downfall

indicators.note: an initial is the first letter of a name

parts.note: the first letter of Trump
rain is a downfall from the sky

explanation.surface: A political commentary on the chain of events that began Trump's fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Downfall' suggests political ruin, but it is weather falling down.
explanation.definitionFit: A train of events or thought is a connected series, a sequence.

clue.text: The endless invasion of a solitary Irish location

indicators.note: an invasion means forcing into the inside of something
endless means losing the final letter

parts.note: taken as written
the word without its last letter
lone and solitary are synonyms

explanation.surface: A history of an endless invasion of a lonely spot in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Athlone is a town in the Irish midlands on the River Shannon, a place in Ireland.

clue.text: Puzzle involving puns, only shortened

indicators.note: shortened means cut down by its last letter
involving suggests tangling up together, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written
the word with its last letter cut

explanation.surface: A crossword described as relying only on brief wordplay jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puzzle' looks like a noun for the crossword itself, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To nonplus someone is to bewilder or perplex them, which is to puzzle them.

clue.text: See 3 Down
It's a big thing, Latin — have to get translated

indicators.note: translated words are turned into another form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A student finds that translating Latin is a huge task.
explanation.definitionFit: A leviathan is a sea monster from the Bible, hence any enormous thing.

clue.text: As a beanpole is set to absorb two fertiliser elements

indicators.note: absorbing means taking something inside oneself

parts.note: to lay is to set down
N is nitrogen and K potassium, both key fertiliser elements

explanation.surface: A gardener's note on feeding a bean plant with fertiliser.
explanation.walkthrough: A beanpole is a tall thin person as well as a garden cane.
explanation.definitionFit: Lanky means tall and thin, exactly how a person nicknamed a beanpole is built.

clue.text: See 5
Month before an attempt to acquire new figure

indicators.note: acquiring something means taking it on at the end

parts.note: OCT is the calendar abbreviation for October
an is the indefinite article A
a go is an attempt
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A dieter plans an attempt to reach a new body shape before next month.
explanation.definitionFit: An octagon is an eight-sided geometric figure, a plane shape.

clue.text: Enjoying continuing success playing a character on the radio

indicators.note: radio is heard and not seen, so the words are taken by their sound

parts.note: an actor playing a character is on a role

explanation.surface: An actor having a streak of good fortune while performing a radio part.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on a roll is an idiom for enjoying a run of success that keeps going.

clue.text: Holding note with Sinatra?

parts.note: te is a note of the sol-fa scale
Nancy Sinatra, the singer and Frank's daughter

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a musical note is being sustained by Sinatra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sinatra' points to Frank, but the needed Sinatra is his daughter Nancy.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenancy is the holding of property as a tenant, so holding in the legal sense.

clue.text: Minor habit condensed from personality

indicators.note: condensed from means drawn out of a longer stretch of text, packed inside it

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A psychologist's note that a small quirk comes from one's character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habit' means a garment, as a nun's habit is; 'minor' means a child.
explanation.definitionFit: Rompers are a one-piece garment worn by small children, so clothing for a minor.
